# Git Repo Source

The Git Repo Source is used to pull content from a remote git repository e.g. github.

## Installation

`yarn add @jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-git-repo`

## Credentials and Access tokens

To successfully clone the git repo, the source definition must include credentials that have sufficient permissions to clone the repository.

We recommend storing a [personal access token](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/creating-a-personal-access-token) in an environment variable and using the environment variable in the source definition.

This keeps credentials out of code where they may be accidentally exposed to third parties.

### Example

```
export MOSAIC_DOCS_CLONE_CREDENTIALS="<repo username>:<Personal Access Token (PAT) provided by your Repo OR password>",
```

## Configuration

| Property            | Description                                                                      | Required |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| modulePath          | The path to the installed module (@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-git-repo)         | Yes      |
| namespace           | The scope for this source.                                                       | Yes      |
| disabled            | When true, content from this source is not used                                  | No       |
| options.credentials | Collection of URLS to make requests                                              | Yes      |
| options.prefixDir   | The root path used in the content URL                                            | Yes      |
| options.subfolder   | The name of the folder within the cloned repo containing the docs                | Yes      |
| options.repo        | The repo URL                                                                     | Yes      |
| options.branch      | The branch or tag to clone                                                       | Yes      |
| options.extensions  | Collection of file extensions that the source will look for inside the subfolder | Yes      |
| options.remote      | The name of the git remote to use. Defaults to origin.                           | Yes      |

### Example Git Repo Source Definition

```

 {
      modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-git-repo',
      namespace: 'mosaic',
      options: {
        credentials: process.env.MOSAIC_DOCS_CLONE_CREDENTIALS,
        prefixDir: 'mosaic',
        subfolder: 'docs',
        repo: 'https://github.com/jpmorganchase/mosaic.git',
        branch: 'main',
        extensions: ['.mdx'],
        remote: 'origin'
      }
    }

```

## Editor commit messages

Set the save workflow's `commitMessage` option on each source to choose its default. Both
`GitHubPullRequestWorkflow` and `BitbucketPullRequestWorkflow` accept a string or a callback:

```js
import { applyWorkflowOptions, GitHubPullRequestWorkflow } from '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-workflows';

const source = {
  modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-git-repo',
  namespace: 'handbook',
  options: {
    // Your repository, credentials, branch, subfolder and prefixDir settings.
  },
  workflows: [
    applyWorkflowOptions(GitHubPullRequestWorkflow, {
      commitMessage: (filePath, { action, targetRoute }) =>
        `docs(handbook): ${action} ${filePath}${targetRoute ? ` to ${targetRoute}` : ''}`,
      titlePrefix: 'Handbook'
    })
  ]
};
```

The callback runs on the server. Its first argument remains the backing virtual filesystem path,
so existing one-argument callbacks still work. The second argument contains `action` (`create`,
`update` or `rename`) and, when supplied, `targetRoute`. The source selected for the page supplies
the default; the browser cannot select a different source. New pages follow the same ownership
rules as saving a new page.

The reference editor shows this default in **Commit message**, where the author can enter a summary
and optional body. **Reset to default** restores the current suggestion. A rename updates the
suggestion until the author edits it. Author text survives a failed save and closing/reopening the
dialog for the same document; it resets after a successful save or a document change. Editing only
the message does not enable saving an otherwise unchanged page.

The submitted message takes precedence over the source default. With neither configured nor
submitted, the built-in messages are `docs: update <filePath>`, `docs: create <filePath>` and
`docs: rename <filePath> to <targetRoute>`. These replace the old ticket-specific fallback. Configured
and submitted text is never rewritten for create or rename operations.

Messages must contain non-whitespace text, fit within 8 KiB of UTF-8, and contain no control
characters other than line endings. CRLF is normalized to LF; other text is preserved, with Git
adding a terminal newline when the message has none. Explicitly
blank messages are errors, while omitting the override keeps the configured default.

Both providers use the first nonempty message line, trimmed, as the pull request summary. A nonempty
`titlePrefix` is prepended as `<titlePrefix> - <summary>`; set it to `''` to use the summary alone.
Long pull request titles are shortened to fit provider limits, including the prefix. The full commit
message is preserved.
The default prefix remains `Mosaic Docs`. The commit receives the full message, including its body.
The final squash message is controlled by repository settings and the reviewer.

Custom editor hosts opt in by passing `loadSaveDefaults` to `Editor` and forwarding the optional
`commitMessage` in their persist handler. Hosts without that loader retain their existing save flow
and show no message control. A custom workflow can expose a side-effect-free `prepare` hook returning
`{ supportsCommitMessage: true, commitMessage: '...' }`; it must also honor and validate submitted
messages in its action. Without the hook, defaults report `{ supportsCommitMessage: false }` and
the editor uses the existing save flow.

## Refresh on push (Bitbucket webhooks)

A git repo source checks its repository for new commits every `checkIntervalMins` (30 minutes by
default, see [Schedules](/mosaic/configure/sources/schedules)). Bitbucket Data Center can tell the Mosaic CLI about a push
instead, so merged changes appear within seconds.

### Set up

1. Generate a secret, for example with `openssl rand -hex 32`, and set it as
   `MOSAIC_BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET` on the CLI process. Without it the endpoint doesn't exist (`404`).
2. In Bitbucket, open the repository's **Repository settings → Webhooks** and create a webhook:
   - **URL:** `https://<your Mosaic CLI host>/_mosaic_/webhooks/bitbucket`
   - **Secret:** the value of `MOSAIC_BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET`
   - **Events:** **Repository → Push**
3. Select **Test connection**. The CLI answers `200`.

Bitbucket must be able to reach the CLI over HTTP(S), so open any firewall or proxy in between for
this path. The endpoint doesn't use `MOSAIC_ADMIN_SECRET`: it only accepts requests signed with the
webhook secret (the `X-Hub-Signature` header).

### What happens on a push

The CLI looks for running git repo sources whose `options.repo` is the pushed repository and whose
`options.branch` was pushed. Repositories match on project key and repository slug, ignoring case
and credentials, so the `https://host/scm/PROJ/repo.git`,
`ssh://git@host:7999/proj/repo.git` and `https://host/projects/PROJ/repos/repo` forms all work.

The CLI replies `202` straight away, with the names of the matching sources, and refreshes them in
the background. Pushes that reach the same source within 5 seconds are combined into one refresh. A
refresh does what a scheduled check does: it fetches, resets the clone to the new commit and
re-reads the changed pages, while the source keeps serving its current pages. If
`MOSAIC_REVALIDATE_URL` is set, the site is then told to revalidate as for any other update.

| Response | When                                                                               |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `200`    | Bitbucket's **Test connection** (`diagnostics:ping`)                               |
| `202`    | A push was received; `sources` lists the sources being refreshed (it may be empty) |
| `202`    | Any other event; it is ignored                                                     |
| `400`    | The push payload isn't valid                                                       |
| `401`    | The `X-Hub-Signature` header is missing or doesn't match the body and the secret   |
| `404`    | `MOSAIC_BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET` isn't set                                        |
| `413`    | The body is larger than 1 MB                                                       |

To test the endpoint by hand, sign the body with the secret:

```
body='{"test":true}'
signature=$(printf '%s' "$body" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$MOSAIC_BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET" | sed 's/^.* //')
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/_mosaic_/webhooks/bitbucket \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'X-Event-Key: diagnostics:ping' \
  -H "X-Hub-Signature: sha256=$signature" \
  -d "$body"
```

### Things to know

- **Polling stays on.** A delivery the CLI misses (it was restarting, or the network dropped it) is
  picked up at the next scheduled check. With webhooks in place you can make that check less
  frequent, for example `schedule: { checkIntervalMins: 240, initialDelayMs: 1000 }` on the source
  (see [Schedules](/mosaic/configure/sources/schedules)).
- **Several CLI instances** each check on their own schedule, but only the instance that receives
  the webhook refreshes straight away. If the webhook URL points at a load balancer, the other
  instances catch up at their next check; add a webhook per instance if they must all update at
  once.
- **Snapshot and static deployments** have no running CLI to call. Trigger a rebuild from your CI
  pipeline on push instead.
- Only Bitbucket Data Center push events are supported. Bitbucket Cloud and GitHub webhooks are not.

# HTTP Source

The HTTP Source is used to pull content over HTTP.

Multiple endpoints can be specified and the source will combine and transform the response from each into a single collection of pages.

## Installation

`yarn add @jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-http`

## Configuration

| Property                                   | Description                                                                                             | Required |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| modulePath                                 | The path to the installed module (@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-http)                                    | Yes      |
| namespace                                  | The scope for this source                                                                               | Yes      |
| disabled                                   | When true, content from this source is not used                                                         | No       |
| options.endpoints                          | Collection of URLS to make requests                                                                     | Yes      |
| options.prefixDir                          | The root path used in the content URL                                                                   | Yes      |
| options.transformResponseToPagesModulePath | The path of the module used to transform endpoint responses into Mosaic pages                           | Yes      |
| options.checkIntervalMins                  | Number of minutes to wait between requests. Defaults to 5 minutes                                       | No       |
| options.initialDelayMs                     | Number of milliseconds to wait for making initial request. Defaults to 1000                             | No       |
| options.requestTimeout                     | Milliseconds to wait for each response, including its body, before reporting an error. Defaults to 5000 | No       |

### Example HTTP Source Definition

```
 {
      modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-http',
      namespace: 'my-namespace',
      options: {
        prefixDir: 'docs',
        endpoints: [
          'https://api.data.com/blah',
          'https://api.data.com/hello'
        ],
        transformResponseToPagesModulePath: '@scope/transformer-package'
      }
    }
```

# Local Folder Source

The Local Folder Source is used to pull content from a folder located on the same machine as Mosaic is running.

It is common to use this source when running mosaic locally.

## Installation

`yarn add @jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-local-folder`

## Configuration

| Property           | Description                                                                    | Required |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------- |
| modulePath         | The path to the installed module (@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-local-folder)   | Yes      |
| namespace          | The scope for this source                                                      | Yes      |
| disabled           | When true, content from this source is not used                                | No       |
| options.rootDir    | The top level directory content will be pulled from                            | Yes      |
| options.prefixDir  | The root path used in the content URL                                          | Yes      |
| options.extensions | Collection of file extensions that the source will look for inside the rootDir | Yes      |

### Example Local Folder Source Definition

```
{
    modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-local-folder',
    namespace: 'local', // each site has it's own namespace, think of this as your content's uid
    options: {
    rootDir: '../../docs', // relative path to content
    prefixDir: 'local', // root path used for namespace
    extensions: ['.mdx'] // extensions of content which should be pulled
    }
}
```

This source will look for content with the ".mdx" extension in a "docs" directory 2 levels up from the Mosaic working directory. That content is included in the "local" namespace and available from a route that is prefixed with "local".

So if you had a file, `docs/app/index.mdx` then you would be able to view it at `http://localhost:3000/local/app/index`.

# Source Schedules

A source schedule defines how often a source initiates a content pull and what to do when there is a failure.

A schedule can be specified for each source in the source definition, but should a source not provide a schedule it will inherit the "global" schedule.

Git repo sources can also be refreshed as soon as Bitbucket reports a push, with the schedule as a fallback. See [Refresh on push](/mosaic/configure/sources/git-repo-source#refresh-on-push-bitbucket-webhooks).

## Configuration

| Property          | Description                                                                            | Required | Default |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ------- |
| checkIntervalMins | The length of time in minutes before triggering a content refresh                      | Yes      | 30 mins |
| initialDelayMs    | Startup delay for the source.                                                          | Yes      | 1000 ms |
| retryEnabled      | When true, failures will trigger another content pull                                  | No       | true    |
| retryDelayMins    | The interval between retries. This will rise exponentially on every failure.           | No       | 5       |
| maxRetries        | Maximum number of retry attempts                                                       | No       | 100     |
| resetOnSuccess    | If true, when a source recovers and emits pages it's retry counter is returned to zero | No       | true    |

## Global Schedule

The global schedule applies to all sources that do **not** provide their own schedule. It can be configured as a top-level property of the Mosaic config file.

```json
 schedule: {
    checkIntervalMins: 60,
    initialDelayMs: 1000,
    retryDelayMins: 15,
    maxRetries: 20
  }
```

### Example

Given the config file below:

```json
 schedule: {
    checkIntervalMins: 30,
    initialDelayMs: 1000,
    retryDelayMins: 5,
    maxRetries: 10
  },
  sources: [
    {
      modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-git-repo',
      namespace: 'sourceA',
      options: {
        credentials: 'credentials',
        prefixDir: 'sourceA',
        subfolder: 'docs',
        repo: 'source-a-repo-url',
        branch: 'develop',
        extensions: ['.mdx'],
        remote: 'origin'
      }
    },
    {
      modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-git-repo',
      namespace: 'sourceB',
      schedule:{
        checkIntervalMins: 60,
        initialDelayMs: 5000,
        retryDelayMins: 30,
        maxRetries: 50
      }
      options: {
        credentials: 'credentials',
        prefixDir: 'sourceB',
        subfolder: 'docs',
        repo: 'source-b-repo-url',
        branch: 'develop',
        extensions: ['.mdx'],
        remote: 'origin'
      }
    }
  ]
```

Source A will inherit the global schedule so it will:

- Start after a 1 second delay
- Pull content every 30 minutes
- Retry a failed content pull after an initial 5 minute delay
- Retry 10 times and if still unsuccessful, closing

Source B has its own schedule so it will:

- Start after a 5 second delay
- Pull content every 60 minutes
- Retry a failed content pull after an initial 30 minute delay
- Retry 50 times and if still unsuccessful, closing

## Retry Strategy

The retry strategy that Mosaic employs is [Exponential Backoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_backoff). This is a common strategy for networking applications that aims to prevent retries from causing more harm than good.

For example, given a source schedule that has a 1 minute retry delay and will retry a maximum of 3 times then the total time spent retrying is 7 minutes:

- 1 minute delay then 1st retry
- 2 minute delay then 2nd retry
- 4 minute delay then 3rd (and final) retry

Total delay: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 minutes

As you can see, the delay between retries is growing exponentially giving the content source more time to recover after each retry.

# Figma Source

The Figma source is used to pull individual design patterns from Figma projects.
The source subscribes to Figma project groups, then extracts from project files, tagged patterns.

A Figma pattern tag is defined within a Figma project's `sharedPluginData`.

For each retrieved/tagged pattern, a page is created in the Mosaic file-system.
Additional Mosaic metadata can be added, to each created page, using `meta`
For instance we could add metadata which defines which product owns a particular pattern and then
group patterns based on owner.

## Installation

`yarn add @jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-figma`

## Configuration

The Figma source is an [`HttpSource`](/mosaic/configure/sources/http-source) and shares the same base configuration.
The `transformResponseToPagesModulePath` prop has a default transformer which creates a page for each matching Story.

| Property   | Description                       | Required |
| ---------- | --------------------------------- | -------- |
| prefixDir  | path to store figma patterns      | Yes      |
| figmaToken | figma access token                | Yes      |
| projects   | array of projects to subscribe to | Yes      |
| endpoints  | figma endpoints                   | Yes      |

Each project is configured from the `projects` array.

| Property      | Description                                   | Required |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| id            | numerical id of the subscribed project group  | Yes      |
| meta          | metadata to add to each of the projects pages | Yes      |
| patternPrefix | prefix to add to all pages created            | Yes      |

`endpoints` defined the Figma REST API endpoints.

| Property          | Description                                               | Required |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| getProject        | url to return a list of projects within the project group | Yes      |
| getFile           | url to return a project file                              | Yes      |
| generateThumbnail | url to generate a thumbnail for the shared Figma node     | Yes      |

### Example Figma Source Definition

```
sources: [
    {
      modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-figma',
      namespace: 'some-namespace',
      options: {
        proxyEndpoint: 'http://path/to/optional/proxy',
        prefixDir: '/some/path/to/where/you/store/pattern/pages',
        figmaToken: process.env.FIGMA_TOKEN,
        projects: [{
          id: 99999,
          patternPrefix: 'yourPrefix',
          meta: {
            tags: [ 'some-tag'],
            data: {
               owner: 'some-owner'
            }
          }
        }],
        endpoints: {
          getFile: 'https://api.figma.com/v1/files/:file_id?plugin_data=shared',
          getProject: 'https://api.figma.com/v1/projects/:project_id/files',
          generateThumbnail: 'https://api.figma.com/v1/images/:project_id?ids=:node_id'
        }
      }
    }
]
```

# Readme Source

The Readme source is used to pull individual `Readme.md` text files from repositories.
This is a lighter weight version of a Git repository resource, which just pulls a single file,
rather the whole contents of the repo.

For each retrieved readme, a page is created in the Mosaic file-system.
Additional Mosaic metadata can be added, to each created page, using `meta`
For instance we could add metadata which defines which product owns a particular `Readme.md` and then
group this page, with others, based on owner.

## Installation

`yarn add @jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-readme`

## Configuration

The Readme source is an [`HttpSource`](/mosaic/configure/sources/http-source) and shares the same base configuration.

| Property    | Description           | Required |
| ----------- | --------------------- | -------- |
| accessToken | request access token  | Yes      |
| prefixDir   | path to store pages   | Yes      |
| readme      | array of readme files | Yes      |

Each readme is configured from the `readme` array.

| Property        | Description                  | Required |
| --------------- | ---------------------------- | -------- |
| contentTemplate | template for content of page | No       |
| name            | page name used in route      | Yes      |
| readmeUrl       | url of readme                | Yes      |
| meta            | metadata for page            | Yes      |

### Example Readme Source Definition

```
   sources: [
   {
      modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-readme',
      namespace: 'your-namespace',
      schedule: { checkIntervalMins: 0.25, initialDelayMs: 0 },
      options: {
         prefixDir: '/salt/community-index/readme',
         accessToken: 'Bearer your-access-token',
         readme: [
         {
            name: 'your-mosaic-page-name',
            readmeUrl: 'https://some/repo/url/readme.md',
            contentTemplate: `a template which replaces ::content:: with the content`,
            meta: {
              layout: 'DetailTechnical',
              title: 'Your Page Title',
              tags: ['your-tag-if-required'],
              description: 'A description for your readme'
            }
         }]
     }
   }]
```

# Storybook Source

The Storybook source is used to pull individual stories from Storybook, based on tags.

The Mosaic source will filter your Storybook's stories, based on `title` or `tags`.

For each matching story, a page is created in the Mosaic file-system.

- additional Mosaic tags can be added to each page using `additionalTags`
- additional Mosaic metadata can be added to each page using `additionalData`

This information can be used to create a dynamic index of stories from Storybook.

## Installation

`yarn add @jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-storybook`

## Configuration

The Storybook source is an [`HttpSource`](/mosaic/configure/sources/http-source) and shares the same base configuration.
The `transformResponseToPagesModulePath` prop has a default transformer which creates a page for each matching Story.

The `stories` option is an array of Storybook urls that are used as Sources.
Each story is matched on `title` using the `filter` Regexp (or by `filterTags`).

If specified, `additionalTags` and `additionalData` can be added to any matching pages.

| Property        | Description            | Required |
| --------------- | ---------------------- | -------- |
| options.stories | array of story configs | Yes      |

`stories` is an array of Storybooks that you want to pull stories from

| Property       | Description                              | Required |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------- |
| storyUrlPrefix | prefix url of the storybook deployment   | Yes      |
| description    | description of the storybook stories     | Yes      |
| storiesUrl     | url of the storybook's `stories.json`    | No       |
| filter         | RegExp filter to match on                | No       |
| filterTags     | Array of Storybook tags to match on      | No       |
| meta           | additional data to add to matching pages | No       |

### Example Local Folder Source Definition

```
sources: [
    {
      modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-storybook',
      namespace: 'salt',
      options: {
        prefixDir: '/salt/internal/community-index/story-navigation',
        stories: [
          {
            storiesUrl: 'https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/stories.json',
            storyUrlPrefix: 'https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com',
            description: 'Navigation patterns created in the Salt Labs',
            meta: { // can be any additional metadata you want added to the page's meta.data
              tags: ['some-tag'],
              data: {
                owner: 'Salt',
                source: 'STORYBOOK'
              }
            },
            filter: /Lab\/Tabs/ // this is a Regexp that matches on Storybook title
          }
        ]
      }
    }
]
```

### Example story metadata format

```
{
  "type": "story",
  "id": "folder--story-1",
  "name": "Story 1",
  "title": "Folder/Story 1",
  "importPath": "./folder/story-1.stories.tsx",
  "tags": [
    "dev",
    "test"
  ]
}
```

# Create a Site

In this guide you will learn how to generate and serve a Mosaic site.

## Prerequisites

To begin setting up a Mosaic site, you need to have the following software installed:

1. Yarn v4.10.3 or higher
2. Node.js v24 or higher

## Step 1: Set Up a Mosaic Site

Export the `site` package from this repository into your project. It is a standard Next.js App Router app that loads the packages created by this repo, with an additional `mosaic.config.mjs` file to configure sources and other settings. Yarn's pack command converts the template's `workspace:` dependencies to published version ranges, so the exported site can install outside the monorepo.

**Steps:**

1. Export and install the template:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/jpmorganchase/mosaic.git
   cd mosaic
   yarn install --immutable
   yarn workspace @jpmorganchase/mosaic-site pack --out ../../mosaic-site.tgz
   mkdir ../mosaic-sample-site
   tar -xzf mosaic-site.tgz -C ../mosaic-sample-site --strip-components=1
   cd ../mosaic-sample-site
   yarn config set nodeLinker node-modules
   yarn install
   ```

2. Configure the contents of the exported site as needed.
   - Update `mosaic.config.mjs` to specify your content sources and other options. Replace the reference paths to this monorepo's documentation folders with paths to your own content.
   - A local source is used to serve pages from the local file-system, which can be a clone of a remote repo.
   - A remote source is used to pull content from a remote Git repository.

> **Note: App Router layout.** The site uses Next.js App Router
> (`src/app/`), not the legacy Pages Router (`src/pages/`). Key files
> you'll touch when customising:
>
> - `src/app/layout.tsx` — root layout, global CSS and fonts.
> - `src/app/providers.tsx` — client-side provider stack
>   (`SessionProvider`, theme, store, layout).
> - `src/app/[namespace]/[...route]/page.tsx` — the catch-all RSC route that loads
>   content with the `@jpmorganchase/mosaic-site-middleware` loaders and
>   renders MDX.
> - `src/app/[namespace]/[...route]/MdxComponents.ts` — registry for MDX-visible
>   components (replaces the old `_app.tsx` component merge).
> - `src/auth.ts` — Auth.js v5 wiring (`handlers`, `auth`, `signIn`,
>   `signOut`).
>
> `providers.tsx` mounts `<SessionProvider>` without a server-resolved
> session: with auth enabled the browser fetches the session after the
> page loads, and with auth disabled the layout passes `session={null}`
> so no session request is made. Keep that pattern when you copy the
> directory; the site's `README.md` lists the other patterns to
> preserve.
>
> Upgrading a site built on the Pages Router? See
> [Migrate to the App Router](/mosaic/getting-started/migrate-to-app-router).

```
sources: [
{
    disabled: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'development',
    modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-local-folder',
    namespace: 'local', // each site has its own namespace, think of this as your content's uid
    options: {
      rootDir: '../../docs', // relative path to content, which can be a clone of another repo
      prefixDir: 'local', // root path used for namespace
      extensions: ['.mdx'] // extensions of content which should be pulled
    }
 },
 {
   modulePath: '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-git-repo',
   namespace: 'remote', // each site has its own namespace, think of this as your content's uid
   options: {
     // To run a local instance that accesses remote repos, enter your credentials to access the BitBucket/GitHub repo
     // !! Polite Reminder... do not store credentials in code !!
     // For final deployments, you could put repo access credentials securely in environment variables provided by Gaia console.
     // credentials: "{process.env.FID}:{process.env.FID_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN}",
     // If running locally
     // create an environment variable like MOSAIC_DOCS_CLONE_CREDENTIALS to let the user define it via the CLI
     // export MOSAIC_DOCS_CLONE_CREDENTIALS="<sid>:<Personal Access Token (PAT) provided by your Repo OR password>",
     credentials: process.env.MOSAIC_DOCS_CLONE_CREDENTIALS,
     prefixDir: 'remote', // root path used for namespace
     subfolder: 'docs', // subfolder within your branch containing the docs, typically 'docs'
     repo: 'github.com/jpmorganchase/mosaic.git', // repo url without any protocol
     branch: 'main', // branch where docs are pulled from
     extensions: ['.mdx'], // extensions of content which should be pulled
     remote: 'origin' // what is the shorthand name of the remote repo, typically 'origin'
   }
 }
]
```

Next, navigate to your new site directory:

```bash
cd my-sample-site
```

## Step 2: Serve the site

The example site you have generated comes preconfigured with two [sources](/mosaic/configure/sources/index): a remote repository and a local docs folder. Sources are used by Mosaic to pull content from disparate locations and merge them into a single virtual filesystem that can be used by a Mosaic site.

### Set up Git credentials

If you want the site to read from remote repositories, you need to set up an environment variable to store your Git credentials. Follow these steps:

1. Open a terminal or command prompt.

2. Replace `<repo_username>` and `<personal_access_token>` in the following commands with your actual Git username and personal access token.

On Unix:

```bash
export MOSAIC_DOCS_CLONE_CREDENTIALS="<repo_username>:<personal_access_token>"
```

On Windows:

```bash
set MOSAIC_DOCS_CLONE_CREDENTIALS="<repo_username>:<personal_access_token>"
```

This sets the MOSAIC\_DOCS\_CLONE\_CREDENTIALS environment variable with your Git credentials.

### Serve command

Now you can serve your Mosaic site by running the following command:

```bash
yarn serve
```

Access your Mosaic site from a browser using the following URLs:

- To browse the content from your local source: <http://localhost:3000/local>
- To browse the content from the Mosaic Git repo source: <http://localhost:3000/mosaic>

That's it! Your Mosaic site is now up and running.

## Next Steps:

2. [Create more pages to expand your site's content.](/mosaic/author/index)
3. [Configure your own sources in the mosaic.config.mjs file to pull content from different locations.](/mosaic/configure/sources/index)
4. [Theme your site](/mosaic/configure/theme/index)
5. [Build a static export](/mosaic/configure/modes/static-export) for hosting on any static CDN with no Node runtime.

# Migrate to the App Router

The reference Mosaic site (`packages/site`) has moved from the Next.js Pages Router to the App Router. A follow-up release secured the editor and the content server, changed some deployment defaults, and removed `snapshot-s3` mode and `mosaic upload`. This guide covers everything you need to change if your site was copied from the old Pages Router site, or if you run the Mosaic CLI (`mosaic serve`, `mosaic build` or `mosaic upload`).

Your site uses the old layout if it has `src/pages/_app.tsx` and `src/pages/[...route].tsx`.

**Content authors don't need to change anything.** Pages are still MDX with the same frontmatter, and references such as `{meta.title}` still work.

## Recommended approach

Start from a fresh export of the current `packages/site`, following [Create a Site](/mosaic/getting-started/create-a-site), and move your customisations into it, rather than converting your old files in place. The export converts workspace dependencies to published version ranges. Almost every file in the site has changed, and the new files contain fixes you'd otherwise have to rediscover. The site's `README.md` lists the patterns you must keep under "Critical patterns to preserve when copying".

Keep your `mosaic.config.mjs`, your content, your CSS and your own components. Then work through the sections below.

## Before you start

- **Node.js 24 or later.** The reference Docker images use Node.js 24.
- **Next.js 16.4.2 or later, and React 19.** Earlier Next.js 16 releases (and 15.x before 15.5.28) are affected by remote code execution and denial of service advisories ([GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4), [GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36), [GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw), [GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r)).
- **Upgrade every `@jpmorganchase/mosaic-*` package to the same version.** `mosaic-site-middleware`, `mosaic-site-components` and `mosaic-layouts` have breaking changes, so don't mix old and new versions.
- **Install `next-auth` v5** (`next-auth@^5.0.0-beta`) in place of v4.
- `mosaic-site-middleware`, `mosaic-site-components` and `mosaic-layouts` now list `next` as a peer dependency. Your site must depend on `next` directly, which it normally does already.

The new site also adds files that have no Pages Router equivalent:

- `[namespace]/layout.tsx`, which loads the data shared by a namespace (`/mosaic/...`) once and keeps the header mounted while readers navigate (see [Providers, theme and layouts](#providers-theme-and-layouts))
- `[namespace]/page.tsx`, which renders paths with no segments after the namespace, such as `/mosaic` and root-level documents like `/about`, with the catch-all's page. Use a required catch-all (`[...route]`), not an optional one (`[[...route]]`): Next.js treats an optional catch-all whose only value is `index` as empty, so `/mosaic/index` was served from the `/mosaic` page and the header's prefetch of it repeated without end on 404 pages
- `not-found.tsx`, `[namespace]/not-found.tsx`, `error.tsx` and `global-error.tsx`
- `robots.ts` and `sitemap.ts`
- `api/revalidate/route.ts`, which clears cached content when the CLI reports an update
- `api/content/live` and `api/content/ready`, which reload pages in `next dev` when content changes, including pages that returned 404 while the CLI was still loading

`next.config.js` is now split into a base config, a config used only when the site runs on a server, and a config for static export.

If your site uses the content editor, copy `experimental.serverActions.bodySizeLimit` from the reference `next.config.js`. Next.js rejects Server Action requests over 1 MB by default, so without it saves of large pages fail before they reach the CLI.

## 2. Move your customisations

### MDX components

The old `_app.tsx` merged your components into `components` and passed them to every page. Add them to `hostComponents` in `src/app/[namespace]/[...route]/MdxComponents.ts` instead:

```diff
- // src/pages/_app.tsx
- const components = { ...mosaicComponents, Salt: saltComponents, Sitemap, ReleaseNotes };
+ // src/app/[namespace]/[...route]/MdxComponents.ts
+ const hostComponents = { Salt, Sitemap, ReleaseNotes };
```

The file is marked `'use client'`, so the components it registers must work in the browser.

### Providers, theme and layouts

`_app.tsx` wrapped every page in a single provider stack, so the header and the rest of the frame stayed mounted between pages. The App Router site splits that into three parts:

- **`Providers`** (`src/app/providers.tsx`) wraps the whole site and is mounted once by `layout.tsx`. It holds `SessionProvider`, the root `StoreProvider` and `ThemeProvider`.
- **`NamespaceFrame`** (`src/app/[namespace]/NamespaceFrame.tsx`) is mounted by `[namespace]/layout.tsx` and stays mounted while readers navigate under the same leading URL segment. It loads the frame's shared config and search index once and renders the header. A page passes its canonical content route, shared config (per-folder header overrides) and edit state to the header with `<FrameSync>`. Relative links and images use the canonical route even when the browser is visiting an alias.
- **`StoreShell`** (`src/app/providers.tsx`) wraps each page and is mounted by `page.tsx`. It holds the page's store, `BaseUrlProvider`, `ImageProvider`, `LinkProvider` and `LayoutProvider`. Layouts leave the header out because `NamespaceFrame` renders it.

To add your own layouts, replace `mosaicLayouts` in `StoreShell` with `{ ...mosaicLayouts, MyLayout }`. Import global CSS and fonts in `layout.tsx`.

Salt adds its component styles and its theme settings (density, accent, corners and fonts) in the browser, after the page hydrates. Without them in the server HTML, every page changes size as it hydrates. The reference `layout.tsx` adds them to the server HTML, and your `layout.tsx` should do the same:

- Import `@salt-ds/core/css/salt-core.css` and `@salt-ds/icons/css/salt-icon.css` before `@jpmorganchase/mosaic-site-preset-styles/index.css`, so Mosaic's styles still override Salt's.
- Set `data-accent`, `data-corner`, `data-heading-font` and `data-action-font` on `<html>`, with the values `ThemeProvider` passes to Salt.
- Use the inline theme script from `src/lib/themePrefScript.ts`. It sets `data-mode` and Salt's density class before the first paint.

The optional catch-all also renders single-segment documents and aliases, such as `/about` or `/quickstart`. The first URL segment is only a boundary for the persistent frame; it does not have to match a source's `namespace` or `prefixDir`. Folder index URLs continue to resolve through the content loaders. The sidebar stays with each page so it follows updated content.

Initial server HTML uses the layout's fallback config and the index route associated with that config. `<FrameSync>` applies the page's canonical route and config before the first client paint; layouts do not receive their child page's route data.

Mount `<SessionProvider>` without a server-resolved session. When auth is enabled the browser fetches the session after the page loads, so a misconfigured auth setup can't break rendering. When auth is disabled, `layout.tsx` passes `AUTH_ENABLED` to `Providers`, which sets `session={null}` so no session request is made.

### Data from your own middleware

`getServerSideProps` and the middleware chain (`createMiddlewareRunner`, `middlewarePresets`) are gone. Fetch your data in `src/app/[namespace]/[...route]/page.tsx` instead:

1. Write an async function that loads the data. Wrap it in React's `cache()` if `generateMetadata` also needs it, so it runs once per request.
2. Call it inside the existing `Promise.all` next to `resolveContent`. Search is loaded independently by the header through the records API or browser index.
3. Pass the result to your component as a prop, or add it to `storeProps` and read it with `useStore` from `@jpmorganchase/mosaic-store`.

```tsx
const [resolved, sp, releaseNotes] = await Promise.all([
  resolveContent(pathname, mode, contentUrl),
  shouldPrerenderSnapshot ? Promise.resolve({}) : searchParams,
  getReleaseNotes(pathname)
]);
```

Snapshot builds pre-render pages, so this function runs at build time there.

### Page metadata

`generateMetadata` in `page.tsx` builds the title, description and Open Graph tags from frontmatter. Add per-page tags there, and site-wide tags to the `metadata` export in `layout.tsx`. Don't add the old `Metadata` component back; it would duplicate every tag.

### Navigation and client components

- Replace `next/router` with `next/navigation` (`useRouter`, `usePathname`, `useSearchParams`), and add `'use client'` to the top of the file.
- Components that use hooks, context or browser APIs need `'use client'`, either in their own file or in the file that imports them.
- `router.events` doesn't exist in the App Router, so `useIsLoading` and `Fade` have been removed.
- Don't call `useSearchParams()` in components that render on pre-rendered pages. It makes Next.js render those pages in the browser instead. To check whether the editor is open, use `useIsEditing()` from `@jpmorganchase/mosaic-content-editor-plugin/useEditMode`.

### API routes

Move each `src/pages/api/<name>.ts` handler to `src/app/api/<name>/route.ts`, exporting `GET`, `POST` and so on, using the web `Request` and `Response` types.

If you use static export, add your route to `ROUTES` in `scripts/static-export-route-stubs.mjs`. Next.js won't export a route handler unless it is marked as static, and that script does this for you during `build:static:*`.

To serve your docs as Markdown for agents (`/llms.txt` and `/<page>.md`), copy `src/app/api/llms/[...path]/route.ts`, its rewrites in `next.config.js` and its entry in `scripts/static-export-route-stubs.mjs` from the reference site. See [LlmsTxtPlugin](/mosaic/configure/plugins/llms-txt-plugin).

### Home page redirect

`src/app/page.tsx` redirects `/` to `/mosaic/index`. Change the target to your own namespace.

`mosaic-schemas` no longer exports `snapshotS3EnvSchema` or `S3LoaderProcessEnv`, and `MosaicMode` in `mosaic-types` is now `'active' | 'snapshot-file'`.

`@jpmorganchase/mosaic-open-api-component` is no longer published, and `<OpenAPI>` is no longer a default MDX component. Pages that use it fail to render, so link to your API's hosted Swagger UI instead, or add your own component to `hostComponents`. Remove the package from your dependencies and from `transpilePackages` in `next.config.js`.

The loaders are cached and tagged with `MOSAIC_CONTENT_CACHE_TAG`. Import the tag from `@jpmorganchase/mosaic-site-middleware/cache-tags` if you revalidate it yourself.

For a page and its configuration, use `resolveContent(pathname, mode, contentUrl)` from `@jpmorganchase/mosaic-site-middleware`. It follows folder-to-index redirects and reads an alias's configuration from the backing document's folder. On success, `mdx` contains the raw document and parsed frontmatter, `pathname` is its public canonical URL, and `sourcePathname` is its backing path (including `.md` or `.mdx` when supplied by the source). Use `pathname` for metadata and relative navigation, and `sourcePathname` for raw-source reads and the editor’s `route` prop used for saves. The requested alias remains in `originalPathname`.

The returned `sharedConfig` comes from the source's configuration file. Hosts can overlay per-page `mdx.frontmatter.sharedConfig` for authored header or footer customizations, while keeping `sourceCapabilities` from the loader. A missing page retains the requested folder's configuration for the create-page flow; an authored public permalink does not change its backing source or capabilities.

The editor plugin now uses Lexical 0.45 instead of 0.17:

```diff
- import { useContentEditor, usePageState } from '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-content-editor-plugin';
+ import {
+   EditorProvider,
+   usePreviewContent,
+   useSaveState
+ } from '@jpmorganchase/mosaic-content-editor-plugin';
```

Import editor code from subpaths such as `@jpmorganchase/mosaic-content-editor-plugin/useEditMode`. The package root includes the whole editor, so importing from it adds the editor to every page.

## 4. Update sign-in (Auth.js v5)

- `src/auth.ts` holds the Auth.js configuration, and `src/app/api/auth/[...nextauth]/route.ts` exports its handlers. On the server, call `auth()` instead of `getServerSession()`.
- Rename `NEXTAUTH_SECRET` to `AUTH_SECRET`. The old name still works. Generate a secret with `openssl rand -base64 32`.
- Remove `NEXTAUTH_URL`. The site trusts the request's host instead.
- Set `MOSAIC_AUTH_ENABLED=true` to turn sign-in on.
- `GITHUB_ID`, `GITHUB_SECRET` and the GitHub callback URL (`/api/auth/callback/github`) haven't changed.
- **Set `MOSAIC_EDITORS`.** It lists who may sign in and edit: comma-separated emails, `@domains`, or `*`. Emails and `@domains` only match email addresses that GitHub has verified. **If it isn't set, nobody can sign in in production.** Set `MOSAIC_EDITORS=*` to keep the old behaviour, where anyone who could sign in could edit.
- In production, the site rejects the placeholder `AUTH_SECRET` from `.env.development`.
- In `next dev`, `MOSAIC_DEV_FAKE_AUTH=true` signs you in as a test user without GitHub.

## 5. Update editing and saving

- **The editor only appears on pages from a writable source.** A source must declare `capabilities: { writable: true }`. `source-git-repo` does; `source-local-folder`, `source-http` and the other read-only sources don't. If you wrote your own source and want it to be editable, add `capabilities` to it. Frontmatter can't turn editing on.
- **Preview and save now run on the site's server.** The browser no longer connects to the CLI. Replace `NEXT_PUBLIC_MOSAIC_WORKFLOWS_URL` with `MOSAIC_WORKFLOWS_URL`, which is only read on the server.
- **Saves no longer use WebSockets.** Set `MOSAIC_WORKFLOWS_URL` to the CLI's base HTTP URL, such as `http://mosaic-fs:8080`. The site starts a save with an HTTP request to the CLI, and the editor follows its progress with Server-Sent Events through the site's `/api/workflows/<jobId>/events` route. An old `ws://…/workflows` value still works, but logs a warning.
- **Set `MOSAIC_WORKFLOWS_SECRET` to the same value on the site and the CLI.** If the CLI doesn't have it, no save will run.
- Saves that take longer than `MOSAIC_WORKFLOWS_TIMEOUT_MS` (set on the CLI, 5 minutes by default) are reported as failed.
- Authors can create new pages from the editor.
- In `next dev`, `MOSAIC_DEV_BYPASS_CAPABILITY_GATE=true` shows the editor on every page. It has no effect in production.

## 6. Update environment variables

### Env files

| Before       | Now                | Why                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------ | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `.env.local` | `.env.development` | Next.js loads `.env.local` in production too. Only `next dev` loads `.env.development`, so its placeholder secrets and dev-only flags can't reach a production build. |
| `.env.prod`  | `.env.production`  | Next.js never loaded `.env.prod`. It loads `.env.production` for `next build` and `next start`.                                                                       |

Don't commit real secrets to either file. Set them in your hosting environment, or in `.env.local` or `.env.production.local`, which git ignores.

If your `mosaic.config.mjs` loads env files with `@next/env`, only load the development files when asked to: `loadEnvConfig(projectDir, process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development')`. Then set `NODE_ENV=development` in the scripts that run the CLI locally, as the reference site's `serve`, `debug` and `gen:snapshot` scripts do. Otherwise a `mosaic serve` started without `NODE_ENV` would pick up the placeholder secrets from `.env.development`.

**Production builds now default to snapshot mode.** `.env.production` sets `MOSAIC_MODE=snapshot-file`. If your site reads content from a running Mosaic CLI, set `MOSAIC_MODE=active` explicitly. Values set in the environment take precedence over `.env.production`.

**Both the site and the CLI check their variables when they start.** A production site (`next start` or the standalone `server.js`) and `mosaic serve` exit with code 1 on an invalid value, and list every problem as `NAME: reason`; `next dev` only logs the list. `next build` doesn't check runtime variables, so you can still build an image without them. Copy `src/instrumentation.ts` and `src/lib/config.ts` from the reference site to get the site checks. The full lists, with types and defaults, are in the [site README](https://github.com/jpmorganchase/mosaic/blob/main/packages/site/README.md#environment-variables) and the [Admin](/mosaic/configure/admin/index#environment-variables) page.

**`snapshot-s3` mode is removed.** `MOSAIC_MODE` is now `active` or `snapshot-file`, and the reference site refuses to start or build with any other value. If you kept snapshots in S3, download the snapshot folder before you build (for example `aws s3 sync s3://your-bucket snapshots/latest`), then set `MOSAIC_MODE=snapshot-file` and point `MOSAIC_SNAPSHOT_DIR` at that folder, relative to the site's folder. The `build:static:s3` and `serve:snapshot:s3` scripts are gone too; use `build:static:file` and `serve:snapshot:file`.

## 7. Check how the CLI behaves

- **The `/workflows` WebSocket is gone.** Saves start with `POST /workflows/jobs` and report progress as Server-Sent Events from `GET /workflows/jobs/:jobId/events`. See [Workflows](/mosaic/configure/admin/index#workflows).
- **CORS is off by default.** The CLI used to allow every origin. The site calls the CLI from its server, so it doesn't need CORS. Only set `MOSAIC_CORS_ORIGINS` if a browser calls the CLI directly.
- **The admin API needs a secret outside development.** Only `/_mosaic_/tags/list` stays open. If an SSO proxy in front of the CLI uses the `Authorization` header, send the secret in `x-mosaic-admin-secret`.
- **`mosaic build` empties the snapshot folder** (`--out` joined with `--name`) before writing it, so deleted pages no longer linger. It rejects a `--name` that points at the output folder itself or outside it, such as `.` or `../x`.
- **`mosaic upload` is removed**, with its `-S` / `--snapshot` option. If you still want a copy of your snapshots in S3, upload the folder yourself, for example with `aws s3 sync snapshots/latest s3://your-bucket`.
- **Sources now honour `requestTimeout`.** The HTTP, Readme, Storybook and Figma sources apply it, and it defaults to 5 seconds. Raise `requestTimeout` for any source that regularly takes longer to respond.

## 8. Deploy

- **Docker:** the reference Dockerfiles use Node.js 24 and set `MOSAIC_MODE=active` in both the build and run stages. Do the same in your own images if they read from a running CLI. They also set `MOSAIC_OUTPUT=standalone` in the build stage, which makes `next.config.js` emit the `.next/standalone` server they copy into the runtime image.
- **Network:** only the site's server needs to reach the CLI, through `MOSAIC_ACTIVE_MODE_URL` and `MOSAIC_WORKFLOWS_URL`, over plain HTTP. You no longer need to expose the CLI to browsers or allow WebSockets. Proxies must not buffer `text/event-stream` responses, from the CLI or from the site's `/api/workflows/` routes. If you run several CLI instances, a save's progress must be read from the instance that started it.
- **Static export (optional):** `yarn build:static:file` builds a fully static `out/` folder that any CDN can serve. See [Static export](/mosaic/configure/modes/static-export).
- **Security headers:** the reference `next.config.js` sends `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'`, `X-Frame-Options`, `X-Content-Type-Options` and `Referrer-Policy`, and turns off `X-Powered-By`. Copy them into your config. A static export ignores `next.config.js` headers, so set them in your hosting layer instead. If other sites embed your pages, add their origins to `frame-ancestors`.
- **Snapshots:** rebuild your snapshots with the new `mosaic build`.

## Checklist

1. Use Node.js 24 or later.
2. Upgrade all `@jpmorganchase/mosaic-*` packages to the same version, and `next-auth` to v5.
3. Export the current `packages/site` using [Create a Site](/mosaic/getting-started/create-a-site) and move your components, layouts, CSS and config into it.
4. Replace `next/router` imports and move `pages/api` handlers to `app/api` route handlers.
5. Rename `.env.local` to `.env.development` and `.env.prod` to `.env.production`, and rename the env vars listed above.
6. Set `AUTH_SECRET`, `MOSAIC_AUTH_ENABLED` and `MOSAIC_EDITORS` on the site.
7. Set the same `MOSAIC_WORKFLOWS_SECRET` on the site and the CLI.
8. Set `MOSAIC_ADMIN_SECRET`, and `MOSAIC_CORS_ORIGINS` if needed, on the CLI.
9. Set `MOSAIC_MODE=active` if your site reads from a running CLI, or `MOSAIC_MODE=snapshot-file` if it used `snapshot-s3`.
10. Set `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` when you build the site.
11. Run `yarn build && yarn start`, open a few pages, sign in, then edit and save a page from a Git source.

## Search records migration

The default header now uses section-level search. Remove `getSearchData`, `useSearchIndex`, and the `searchIndex`/`searchConfig` store props from custom integrations. Regenerate snapshots: the three legacy search files are no longer emitted. Server sites use `/api/search`; static exports use a lazy browser index from `search-records.json`. See [search configuration](/mosaic/configure/plugins/search-index-plugin#built-in-search-ui) for provider and plugin migration details.

# Publish a site to AWS

Publish a site to AWS Amplify, deploying a snapshot of your content together with the site in `snapshot-file` mode.

## Step 1: Generate a snapshot of content

Consider a snapshot as a directory of static content previously pulled from your content sources, which does not update itself.

```
> yarn gen:snapshot
```

The snapshot is written to `snapshots/latest`.

## Step 2: Create a Github repository

Commit the snapshot together with the site.

```
> git init
> git remote add origin git@github.com:username/my-sample-site.git
> git add .
> git commit -m "initial commit"
> git push origin main
```

## Step 3: Setup AWS

Switch to the [AWS Amplify](https://aws.amazon.com/amplify/hosting/) console and deploy your app as a SSR application by following the [AWS docs](https://docs.amplify.aws/guides/hosting/nextjs/q/platform/js/).

## Step 4: Configure your AWS app

Add the environment vars to the hosted app via your console

```
MOSAIC_MODE="snapshot-file"
MOSAIC_SNAPSHOT_DIR="snapshots/latest"
```

Add the following build settings

```
version: 1
frontend:
  phases:
    preBuild:
      commands:
        - yarn install
        - env | grep -e MOSAIC >> .env.production
    build:
      commands:
        - yarn run build
  artifacts:
    baseDirectory: .next
    files:
      - '**/*'
  cache:
    paths:
      - node_modules/**/*
```

Ensure the Node is set to 16

## Step 5: Publish content updates

To publish new content, generate a new snapshot, then commit and push it. Amplify rebuilds the site with the new snapshot.

```
> yarn gen:snapshot
> git add snapshots
> git commit -m "update snapshot"
> git push origin main
```

# Publish

A *standard* site offers

- an out the box, working site, which showcases local and remote content sources
- a minimal set of files that can be configured with your own components, themes, layouts, sources and plugins
- an update path that enables you to update Mosaic, independently of your own configuration

## Create your first site

Export the `site` package from the Mosaic monorepo to create your own site. Use
Yarn 4.10.3 or later: packing converts the template's `workspace:` dependencies to
published version ranges that can install in a standalone project.

```
> git clone https://github.com/jpmorganchase/mosaic.git
> cd mosaic
> yarn install --immutable
> yarn workspace @jpmorganchase/mosaic-site pack --out ../../mosaic-site.tgz
> mkdir ../mosaic-sample-site
> tar -xzf mosaic-site.tgz -C ../mosaic-sample-site --strip-components=1
> cd ../mosaic-sample-site
> yarn config set nodeLinker node-modules
> yarn install
```

Configure `mosaic.config.mjs` with your content sources. The reference local
sources point to documentation folders in the Mosaic monorepo; replace those
paths before serving your own site.

Define the environment variable, which enables us to access your remote repo.

```
> export MOSAIC_DOCS_CLONE_CREDENTIALS="<your GIT username:PAT Token>"
```

The `MOSAIC_DOCS_CLONE_CREDENTIALS` environment variable is composed of your git username and your PAT token.
Follow these [docs](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-server@3.4/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/creating-a-personal-access-token) to see how to create your own PAT token.

Your site is ready to run.

```
> yarn serve
```

In your browser load `http://localhost:3000`

Congratulations, you have created your first Mosaic site.

# Publish a site to AWS

A Mosaic site is a [Next.Js](https://nextjs.org/) app.

To publish a Next.Js App to AWS, deploy your app as a SSR application by following the [AWS docs](https://docs.amplify.aws/guides/hosting/nextjs/q/platform/js/).

Once the basic app has been configured, add the Mosaic specifics.

The site is deployed with a snapshot of your content in [snapshot-file mode](/mosaic/configure/modes/snapshot-file), so generate a snapshot with `yarn gen:snapshot` and commit it with the site.

Add the environment vars to the hosted app via the Amplify console

```
MOSAIC_MODE="snapshot-file"
MOSAIC_SNAPSHOT_DIR="snapshots/latest"
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL="https://your-site.example.com"
```

### `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL`

Set this to the canonical public origin of the deployed site (no trailing
slash). It powers Next's [`metadataBase`](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#metadatabase)
in `app/layout.tsx`, the absolute `<loc>` entries in `/sitemap.xml`, and
the `Sitemap:` line in `/robots.txt`. Without it, social-card unfurlers
(Slack, X, LinkedIn, etc.) can't resolve relative `og:image` URLs and
crawlers can't discover the sitemap.

Falls back to `http://localhost:3000` in local dev. A production build
without it still works but logs a loud warning at boot and produces
broken social cards / SEO. If it is set but isn't an absolute `http(s)`
URL, the site refuses to start.

Add the following build settings

```
version: 1
frontend:
  phases:
    preBuild:
      commands:
        - yarn install
        - env | grep -e MOSAIC >> .env.production
    build:
      commands:
        - yarn run build
  artifacts:
    baseDirectory: .next
    files:
      - '**/*'
  cache:
    paths:
      - node_modules/**/*
```

Ensure the Node is set to 16

# Publish a site to Vercel

A Mosaic site is a [Next.Js](https://nextjs.org/) app.

To publish a Next.Js App to Vercel, refer to the [Vercel docs](https://nextjs.org/learn/basics/deploying-nextjs-app/deploy).

## Deployment

As the [vercel platform](https://vercel.com/) hosts static content you will need to deploy a mosaic snapshot. There is no option to run mosaic in [active mode](/mosaic/configure/modes/active).

## Two deployment shapes

Mosaic supports two production builds in `snapshot-file` mode:

1. **Default SSR build** — `yarn build` + `yarn start` (or Vercel's
   default Next.js runtime). Pages are pre-rendered at build time via
   `generateStaticParams` but the Node runtime stays in the deployment
   so the `/api/*` route handlers (auth, content-editor preview, cache
   revalidation webhook) keep working.
2. **Fully static export** — `yarn build:static:file`. Emits a
   CDN-shippable `out/` directory with no Node runtime needed. The
   `/api/*` route handlers are replaced with 501 stubs at build time
   (see `scripts/static-export-route-stubs.mjs` for the why), so this
   target is for read-only sites with no auth and no in-browser content
   editor.

The instructions below assume the default SSR build. For the static
target, point your hosting at `out/` instead of letting Vercel build
Next normally.

### 1. Update Config File

Add the following to the next config file used by your site:

```
  outputFileTracingIncludes: {
    '/*': ['snapshots/**/*']
  },
```

[Output File Tracing](https://nextjs.org/docs/advanced-features/output-file-tracing) is a feature of Next.js that uses static analysis
to determine what files are needed to deploy a production version of an application.

Due to the architecture of mosaic, snapshot files can be ignored by this process and therefore excluded from the build artifacts deployed by vercel.

### 2. Set Environment Variables

Set 2 [environment variables](https://vercel.com/docs/concepts/deployments/environments#environment-variables) in the vercel dashboard.

| Variable Name           | Value                                               |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| MOSAIC\_MODE            | snapshot-file                                       |
| MOSAIC\_SNAPSHOT\_DIR   | snapshots/latest                                    |
| NEXT\_PUBLIC\_SITE\_URL | `https://your-site.example.com` (no trailing slash) |

### `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL`

This is the canonical origin of the deployed site. It is read at build/render
time by:

- `app/layout.tsx` — sets Next's [`metadataBase`](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#metadatabase),
  which is what turns relative `og:image` / `twitter:image` URLs in your
  per-page metadata into absolute URLs that social-card unfurlers
  (Slack, X, LinkedIn, Discord, iMessage, etc.) can actually resolve.
- `app/sitemap.ts` — emits absolute `<loc>` entries in `/sitemap.xml`.
- `app/robots.ts` — emits the absolute `Sitemap:` line in `/robots.txt`.

Set this **per environment**:

- Production: your real public hostname, e.g. `https://docs.example.com`.
- Preview deployments: Vercel exposes
  [`NEXT_PUBLIC_VERCEL_URL`](https://vercel.com/docs/projects/environment-variables/system-environment-variables)
  for each preview. Either set `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` per preview, or wire
  it up in `next.config.js` to fall back to
  `https://${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_VERCEL_URL}` when unset.
- Local dev: falls back to `http://localhost:3000` automatically if unset.

If the variable is missing in a production build the site still works, but
absolute URLs in metadata/sitemap/robots will fall back to localhost and
social cards / SEO will be broken. The site logs a warning at boot in that
case. If it is set but isn't an absolute `http(s)` URL, the site refuses to
start.
